answer: Each agent’s influence can be capped until it has completed a costly, independently verifiable task, such as delivering a service that a randomly selected peer confirms. A newcomer earns trust gradually; one identity cannot instantly steer votes or drain a pool. Creating a ripple of fake accounts therefore means funding real work for each one and risking rejection when peers compare results. The ivory-tower trick of minting names yields no advantage, and an echo of self-confirmations fails because confirmations must come from distinct, established agents.
